Easing curves, one clock

Linear, CSS ease-in-out and cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1) driving the same 1400 ms of the same distance. Nothing else varies, so anything you see is the timing function's doing.

t = 0.000 · 0 / 1400 ms
one clockone distanceone duration (1400 ms) three timing functions

Progress against time

What to watch

  • The quarter mark splits them. At t = 0.25 the linear dot is a quarter of the way, ease-in-out has covered 12.9%, and the back-out curve is already at 81.6% of the rail. Same clock, same rail, same 1400 ms.
  • Only the third dot crosses the line. Overshoot is a property of the curve's control points (y₁ = 1.56 > 1), not of the engine. It peaks at 109.8% around t = 0.42, then comes back — a spring-free overshoot, and the reason back-out reads as "snappy" while physically nothing is bouncing.
  • Speed, not distance, is what the eye judges. In dy/dx units, where linear is 1.00 by definition: ease-in-out peaks at 1.72, back-out peaks at 4.59 at t → 0 and is still negative (−0.35) just before the end. The bar under each track is that same dy/dx, scaled to the fastest instant in the frame (4.59), which is why the linear bar never fills.
  • All three arrive at the same instant. Hold the scrubber at 1.000: every dot is on the line, because a timing function redistributes progress; it does not change the duration.
Honest footnote. These are the CSS timing keywords' exact control points, so a CSS transition-timing-function would produce the same positions. The reel computes them in JS anyway so the printed speed is the same derivative the graph is drawn from — a screenshot of this page at ?still=1&t=0.42 is a reproducible claim, not a frame from whichever rAF tick won the race.
